```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(boot)
library(mgcv)
library(moments)

data <- read_csv("data/data-train.csv")

raw_moments <- t(as.matrix(select(data, R_moment_1:R_moment_4)))
central <- raw2central(rbind(1, raw_moments))

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    mean = R_moment_1,
    variance = central[3, ],
    sd = sqrt(variance),
    skewness = central[4, ] / sd ^ 3,
    kurtosis = central[5, ] / sd ^ 4,
    Re_f = factor(Re),
    Fr_f = factor(Fr),
    log_St = log(St),
    log_St_sq = log(St)^2,
    log_St_cubic = log(St)^3,
    group = interaction(Re_f, Fr_f, drop = TRUE)
  )

response_labels <- c(mean = "Mean", sd = "Standard deviation", skewness = "Skewness", kurtosis = "Kurtosis")
responses <- set_names(names(response_labels))

range_ratio <- map_dbl(responses, \(r) max(data[[r]]) / min(data[[r]]))
skew_raw <- map_dbl(responses, \(r) skewness(data[[r]]))
skew_log <- map_dbl(responses, \(r) skewness(log(data[[r]])))
```

```{r}
candidates <- c(
  "Baseline (additive)" = "log_St + Re_f + Fr_f",
  "Interaction Model 1" = "log_St * (Re_f + Fr_f) + Re_f:Fr_f",
  "Interaction Model 2" = "log_St + Re_f * Fr_f",
  "Cubic Model" = "log_St + log_St_sq + log_St_cubic
                            + Re_f * Fr_f",
  "Natural spline (3 df)" = "splines::ns(log_St, df = 3) + Re_f * Fr_f",
  "Natural spline (4 df)" = "splines::ns(log_St, df = 4) + Re_f * Fr_f",
  "Natural spline (5 df)" = "splines::ns(log_St, df = 5) + Re_f * Fr_f"
)
model_formula <- \(r, rhs) as.formula(paste0("log(", r, ") ~ ", str_squish(rhs)))

loocv_lm <- expand_grid(model = names(candidates), response = responses) |>
  mutate(
    mse = map2_dbl(model, response, \(m, r)
      cv.glm(data, glm(model_formula(r, candidates[[m]]), data = data))$delta[1]),
    n_par = map_dbl(model, \(m) lm(model_formula("mean", candidates[[m]]), data = data)$rank)
  )

gam_candidates <- c(
  "Common GAM (k = 4)" = "Re_f * Fr_f + s(log_St, k = 4)",
  "Common GAM (k = 5)" = "Re_f * Fr_f + s(log_St, k = 5)",
  "Common GAM (k = 6)" = "Re_f * Fr_f + s(log_St, k = 6)"
)
gam_formula <- \(r, rhs) model_formula(r, rhs)
loocv_gam <- expand_grid(model = names(gam_candidates), response = responses) |>
  mutate(
    mse = map2_dbl(model, response, \(m, r) mean(map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(data)), \(i)
      (log(data[[r]][i]) - predict(gam(gam_formula(r, gam_candidates[[m]]),
                                      data = data[-i, ], method = "REML"), data[i, ]))^2))),
    n_par = map_dbl(model, \(m) round(sum(gam(gam_formula("mean", gam_candidates[[m]]),
                                             data = data, method = "REML")$edf), 1))
  )

loocv <- bind_rows(loocv_lm, loocv_gam)
cv <- loocv |>
  select(model, response, mse) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = response, values_from = mse) |>
  column_to_rownames("model")

fits_baseline <- map(responses, \(r) lm(model_formula(r, candidates[["Baseline (additive)"]]), data = data))
fits_cubic <- map(responses, \(r) lm(model_formula(r, candidates[["Cubic Model"]]), data = data))
final_gam_rhs <- gam_candidates[["Common GAM (k = 5)"]]
fits <- map(responses, \(r) gam(gam_formula(r, final_gam_rhs), data = data, method = "REML"))
r_squared <- map_dbl(fits, \(m) summary(m)$r.sq)
```

```{r}
boxcox_profile <- \(fit, r) {
  raw_fit <- lm(update(formula(fit), paste(r, "~ .")), data = data, y = TRUE)
  p <- MASS::boxcox(raw_fit, lambda = seq(-2, 2, by = 0.01), plotit = FALSE)
  tibble(lambda = p$x, loglik = p$y - max(p$y))
}

bc_profiles <- imap(fits_cubic, boxcox_profile)
bc <- map_dfr(bc_profiles, \(p) {
  ci <- range(p$lambda[p$loglik > -qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2])
  tibble(lambda = p$lambda[which.max(p$loglik)], lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}, .id = "response")
```

# Introduction

This case study explores how three factors affect the clustering of inertial particles in turbulent flows such as clouds. The data come from computer simulations: in each run, our collaborators simulated particles moving in a turbulent flow, identified clusters of particles, and measured the volume of each cluster. The dataset has 89 simulation runs, each summarizing the distribution of particle cluster volumes at one $(Re, Fr, St)$ setting. The three parameters take the following values:

* **Reynolds number** $Re$: 90, 224, 398. This measures how strong the turbulence is.
* **Froude number** $Fr$: 0.052, 0.3, $\infty$. This measures the strength of gravity. Smaller $Fr$ means stronger gravity, and $Fr = \infty$ means no gravity.
* **Stokes number** $St$: `r n_distinct(data$St)` values between `r min(data$St)` and `r max(data$St)`. This measures particle inertia. Particles with small $St$ follow the flow closely, while particles with large $St$ are heavier and respond more slowly.

Our key research objectives are:

1. **Prediction:** predict the first 4 moments of the cluster-volume distribution at new $(Re, Fr, St)$ settings as a fast substitute for running a new simulation. Full computer simulations are expensive and slow: a full run for a single $(Re, Fr, St)$ setting can take days or longer, while a fitted statistical model returns a prediction in seconds. A good predictive model lets our collaborators explore new parameter settings almost instantly instead of waiting for days.
2. **Inference:** Explaining how each parameter affects the response

Our final model is a separate generalized additive model for each response. Here $Re_{224}$, $Re_{398}$, $Fr_{0.3}$, and $Fr_{\infty}$ are 0/1 indicators for each level (baseline $Re = 90$, $Fr = 0.052$), and $f$ is one smooth function shared across the observed $(Re, Fr)$ settings.

$$
\log{\text{response}} = \beta_0 + \alpha_{Re} + \gamma_{Fr} + \delta_{Re \times Fr} + f(\log{St}) + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2).
$$

A separate model is fit for each of the 4 response variables, so each one has its own coefficients and smooth. There is no $Re_{398} Fr_{0.3}$ term because the dataset has no observations at $Re = 398$, $Fr = 0.3$.

This model addresses both objectives. For prediction, it achieves a LOOCV MSE of `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(unlist(cv["Common GAM (k = 5)", ])))` when averaged across the 4 response variables. For inference, the categorical terms describe differences among $Re$ and $Fr$ settings, while the smooth allows the effect of $St$ to vary across its range.

# Methodology

## Responses and predictors

Each observation in the dataset reports the first four raw moments of the response distribution, which we converted to central moments with `raw2central`. From these we computed the mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis of each distribution, which are the 4 desired response variables.

## Transformations

The 4 responses differ in range and in skewness, so we checked each separately, before and after a log transform (@fig-skew in the appendix). The mean and standard deviation span `r format(round(range_ratio[["mean"]]), big.mark = ",")`-fold and `r format(round(range_ratio[["sd"]]), big.mark = ",")`-fold ranges and are strongly right-skewed, with skewness `r sprintf("%.2f", skew_raw[["mean"]])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", skew_raw[["sd"]])`. The log reduces both, to `r sprintf("%.2f", skew_log[["mean"]])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", skew_log[["sd"]])`, although the standard deviation stays moderately right-skewed. Skewness and kurtosis behave differently. Skewness spans only a `r format(round(range_ratio[["skewness"]]), big.mark = ",")`-fold range and is nearly symmetric (`r sprintf("%.2f", skew_raw[["skewness"]])`), and kurtosis spans a `r format(round(range_ratio[["kurtosis"]]), big.mark = ",")`-fold range but is only mildly right-skewed (`r sprintf("%.2f", skew_raw[["kurtosis"]])`). The log over-corrects both into left skew (`r sprintf("%.2f", skew_log[["skewness"]])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", skew_log[["kurtosis"]])`). A single log transform therefore might not suit all four responses equally well.

To investigate this, we fit separate Box-Cox transforms to each response. The resulting $\hat\lambda$ ranges from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(bc$lambda))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(bc$lambda))`, and every 95% interval contains 0 (@tbl-boxcox and @fig-boxcox), which corresponds to log transformations, so the data supports the use of log transformations on all 4 responses.

We also log-transformed $St$ because it is right-skewed (skewness of `r sprintf("%.2f", skewness(data$St))`), spans a wide range, and generally yielded better empirical models when transformed.

## Modeling

We compared the cubic polynomial to natural cubic splines and GAMs. Cubic polynomials can behave poorly near the boundary of the design, whereas a natural spline is constrained to be linear beyond its boundary knots and a GAM controls curvature with a smoothing penalty. All nonlinear candidates use a common $St$ curve plus a $Re \times Fr$ interaction. We deliberately did not retain the earlier group-specific GAM, which estimated a separate curve for each $(Re, Fr)$ group and was too flexible for only 14 observed $St$ values.

All models predict the log of each response. The baseline model has no interaction terms. Interaction Model 1 adds interactions of $\log{St}$ with both $Re$ and $Fr$, as well as $Re \times Fr$. Interaction Model 2 adds only $Re \times Fr$. The cubic and natural-spline candidates add increasingly flexible common $St$ effects to Interaction Model 2. We tuned natural-spline degrees of freedom (3, 4, and 5) and the GAM basis dimension ($k=4,5,6$) by LOOCV; REML selects the GAM's smoothing penalty within each training fold.


Averaged across the 4 response variables, the LOOCV MSE was `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(unlist(cv["Baseline (additive)", ])))` for the baseline model, `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(unlist(cv["Interaction Model 2", ])))` for the $Re \times Fr$ model, `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(unlist(cv["Cubic Model", ])))` for the cubic, and `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(unlist(cv["Common GAM (k = 5)", ])))` for the selected GAM. The GAM with $k=5$ had the lowest average LOOCV MSE and avoided the cubic's boundary behavior, so we selected it as our final model. The table reports the full tuning comparison for each response.

```{r}
loocv |>
  group_by(response) |>
  mutate(cell = if_else(mse == min(mse), sprintf("\\textbf{%.4f}", mse), sprintf("%.4f", mse))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(Model = model, Parameters = n_par, response, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = response, values_from = cell) |>
  rename(!!!set_names(responses, response_labels)) |>
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
        caption = "Comparison of LOOCV MSE accross different models")
```

For the GAM, the parameter count is its effective degrees of freedom; it is reported for the mean model as a compact reference because REML can select slightly different smoothness for the other responses.

$Re$ and $Fr$ each have only 3 levels, so we treat them as categorical.

## Diagnostics

The selected GAM fits all 4 response variables well, with $R^2$ between `r sprintf("%.3f", min(r_squared))` and `r sprintf("%.3f", max(r_squared))`. The plots below compare the residuals of the baseline model (top) and the selected GAM (bottom).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 1.7
#| fig-width: 7
map_dfr(list(Baseline = fits_baseline, "Final model" = fits), \(fit_list)
  imap_dfr(fit_list, \(m, r) tibble(response = response_labels[[r]], fitted = fitted(m), residual = resid(m))),
  .id = "model") |>
  mutate(response = factor(response, levels = response_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, color = "#012169") +
  facet_grid(model ~ response, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (log scale)", y = "Residual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The baseline residuals show clear patterns, especially for skewness and kurtosis, where whole groups of observations sit above or below 0. This means the effect of $Re$ depends on $Fr$. The selected GAM accounts for this interaction and curvature in $St$; its residuals are centered around 0, although some variation in spread remains, particularly for standard deviation.

The residual distributions still depart from normality, especially in their tails. The penalized smooth allows the fitted relationship to bend across the observed $St$ range, but observations at $St = 0.05$ remain worth monitoring because this is the boundary of the design. We kept these observations because there is no sign they are errors.

The dataset was collected from computer simulation runs, but observations with the same $Re$ and $Fr$ likely come from the same simulation, so they may not be fully independent. This could make our uncertainty estimates slightly too small.

# Results

```{r}
test <- read_csv("data/data-test.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Re_f   = factor(Re, levels = levels(data$Re_f)),
         Fr_f   = factor(Fr, levels = levels(data$Fr_f)),
         log_St = log(St),
         log_St_sq = log(St)^2,
         log_St_cubic = log(St)^3)

preds <- imap_dfc(fits, \(fit, r) {
  p <- predict(fit, newdata = test, se.fit = TRUE)
  prediction_se <- sqrt(p$se.fit^2 + fit$sig2)
  tibble(!!r := as.numeric(exp(p$fit)),
         !!paste0(r, "_lower") := as.numeric(exp(p$fit - qnorm(0.975) * prediction_se)),
         !!paste0(r, "_upper") := as.numeric(exp(p$fit + qnorm(0.975) * prediction_se)))
})

test_out <- bind_cols(test |> select(St, Re, Fr), preds)
interval_ratios <- map_dbl(responses, \(r)
  mean(test_out[[paste0(r, "_upper")]] / test_out[[paste0(r, "_lower")]]))
write_csv(test_out, "predictions.csv")
```

## Predictions on the hold-out set

We predicted the four statistics at the `r nrow(test)` hold-out settings, with 95% prediction intervals computed on the log scale and then exponentiated, so point predictions estimate medians. All values are provided in `predictions.csv`. Every hold-out setting uses an $(Re, Fr)$ combination and $St$ value within the training range, so no prediction requires extrapolation. The two settings with $St = 0.05$ lie at the boundary of the observed range and should be interpreted with that limitation in mind.

The precision of the predictions varies across the four statistics. Across the hold-out settings, the upper bounds are about `r sprintf("%.1f", interval_ratios[["mean"]])` times the lower bounds for the mean, `r sprintf("%.1f", interval_ratios[["sd"]])` times for standard deviation, `r sprintf("%.1f", interval_ratios[["skewness"]])` times for skewness, and `r sprintf("%.1f", interval_ratios[["kurtosis"]])` times for kurtosis. The mean is predicted most precisely, while the standard deviation and kurtosis intervals are widest.

## Effects of each parameter

Because the model is fit on the log scale, exponentiating a contrast gives the multiplicative change in a statistic. Since $Re$ and $Fr$ interact, the gravity contrast at a given $Re$ combines the $Fr$ coefficient with the corresponding interaction coefficient. The smooth term means the effect of $St$ varies across its range rather than remaining a constant multiplier.

```{r}
#| label: fig-effects
#| fig-cap: "Fitted values from the final model (lines) and observed data (points). Both axes are on a log scale."
#| fig-height: 1.7
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-pos: "t"
grid <- expand_grid(St = exp(seq(log(0.05), log(3), length.out = 50)),
                    Re = c(90, 224, 398), Fr = c(0.052, 0.3, Inf)) |>
  filter(!(Re == 398 & Fr == 0.3)) |>
  mutate(Re_f = factor(Re, levels = levels(data$Re_f)),
         Fr_f = factor(Fr, levels = levels(data$Fr_f)),
         log_St = log(St),
         log_St_sq = log(St)^2,
         log_St_cubic = log(St)^3)

pred_grid <- imap_dfr(fits, \(m, r) grid |>
  mutate(response = response_labels[[r]], value = exp(predict(m, grid))))

obs <- data |>
  select(St, Re_f, Fr_f, all_of(unname(responses))) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(unname(responses)), names_to = "r", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(response = unname(response_labels[r]))

bind_rows(pred_grid, obs) |>
  mutate(response = factor(response, levels = response_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(St, value, color = Re_f)) +
  geom_line(data = \(d) filter(d, is.na(r)), aes(linetype = Fr_f)) +
  geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, !is.na(r)), aes(shape = Fr_f), size = 0.7) +
      scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = \(x) sapply(x, \(v) format(v, scientific = FALSE,
                big.mark = ",", drop0trailing = TRUE, trim = TRUE))) +
  facet_wrap(~ response, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "St (log scale)", y = "Value (log scale)",
       color = "Re", linetype = "Fr", shape = "Fr") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-st-effect
#| fig-cap: "Estimated partial effect of particle inertia on the log of each response. Shading is an approximate 95% confidence band; zero is the average smooth effect."
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-width: 7
st_grid <- tibble(
  St = exp(seq(log(min(data$St)), log(max(data$St)), length.out = 100)),
  Re_f = factor(90, levels = levels(data$Re_f)),
  Fr_f = factor(0.052, levels = levels(data$Fr_f))
) |>
  mutate(log_St = log(St))

st_effects <- imap_dfr(fits, \(fit, r) {
  p <- predict(fit, st_grid, type = "terms", terms = "s(log_St)", se.fit = TRUE)
  tibble(St = st_grid$St, response = response_labels[[r]],
         effect = p$fit[, 1], se = p$se.fit[, 1])
}) |>
  mutate(lower = effect - qnorm(0.975) * se,
         upper = effect + qnorm(0.975) * se,
         response = factor(response, levels = response_labels))

ggplot(st_effects, aes(St, effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "#6baed6", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(color = "#012169") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ response, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "St (log scale)", y = "Partial effect on log response") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

**Turbulence intensity ($Re$) controls cluster size.** The GAM's fitted contrasts show that increasing $Re$ from 90 to 398 markedly shrinks mean cluster volume and standard deviation, with the reduction in standard deviation weaker under no gravity. Thus, $Re$ has a large association with cluster scale. Under strong gravity, its estimated effects on skewness and kurtosis are comparatively small in this model.

**Strong gravity creates heavy tails, but only when turbulence is weak.** At $Re = 90$, the fitted gravity contrasts show much higher skewness and kurtosis under strong gravity ($Fr = 0.052$) than under no gravity ($Fr = \infty$). Strong gravity is therefore associated with a distribution having many small clusters and occasional very large ones. This effect weakens as $Re$ increases. One physical interpretation is that as turbulence strengthens, turbulent velocity fluctuations overwhelm gravitational settling, so the flow rather than gravity determines how particles cluster.

**Moderate gravity behaves like no gravity.** In the GAM, the fitted effects for $Fr = 0.3$ and $Fr = \infty$ are similar across the four responses. Within the range studied, gravity is most strongly associated with clustering outcomes when it is strong.

**Particle inertia ($St$) has a curved association with the responses.** The selected smooths (Figure @fig-st-effect) allow the relationship between $St$ and each statistic to change in slope across the observed range. A single percentage change for doubling $St$ would therefore be misleading; the confidence bands show where each response-specific curve is most and least precisely estimated. The model uses a common curve across $(Re, Fr)$ settings, while allowing the levels of the curves to differ by those settings.

# Conclusion

Each parameter shapes the cluster-size distribution in a different way. Turbulence intensity is strongly associated with cluster scale, while strong gravity is associated with heavier tails when turbulence is weak. The GAM also indicates that the association with particle inertia changes across the observed $St$ range. Because gravity's influence varies with turbulence strength, conclusions drawn at one turbulence level should not be assumed to hold at another. The model predicts mean cluster volume most precisely; uncertainty is wider for the other statistics.

## Limitations and future work

**The model can only predict at the 3 simulated levels of $Re$ and $Fr$.** Because it treats $Re$ and $Fr$ as categorical, it cannot interpolate intermediate values between levels or extrapolate to more extreme values than simulated. Mapping an unseen input level to the nearest simulated level would let the model perform prediction, but the offset would be completely discarded, and per-unit inference would still be impossible. The model also has no runs at $Re = 398$, $Fr = 0.3$, so interaction effects at that combination cannot be modeled.

**Future simulations should be spread off the grid.** The current runs form a 3 by 3 grid in $(Re, Fr)$ with one combination missing. A more random non-grid structure to selecting input values would be beneficial, allowing $Fr$ and $Re$ to be treated as continuous, which they are. This change will improve interpolation and extrapolation. To address $Fr = \infty$ on a continuous scale, a $1/Fr$ transformation could be introduced.

# Appendix: Exploratory Data Analysis

## Data Processing

We see that the existing data contains Re and Fr values that are collected at distinct levels with low cardinality, instead of continuous values. It includes a valid infinity value for one of the predictors that is not a result of missing data. We compute standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis from raw moments.

```{r}
train_path <- "data/data-train.csv"
raw <- read_csv(train_path, na = c("", "NA"), show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# predictor value distribution
level_table <- function(x, nm) {
  tibble(level = as.character(x)) |>
    count(level, name = "n") |>
    mutate(predictor = nm, .before = 1)
}
predictor_levels <- bind_rows(level_table(raw$Re, "Re"),
                              level_table(raw$Fr, "Fr"))
predictor_levels |>
  kable()

# compute central moments + summary stats
m1 <- raw$R_moment_1
m2 <- raw$R_moment_2
m3 <- raw$R_moment_3
m4 <- raw$R_moment_4

analysis <- raw |>
  mutate(
    variance = m2 - m1^2,
    mean = m1,
    sd = sqrt(variance),
    central_moment_3 = m3 - 3 * m2 * m1 + 2 * m1^3,
    central_moment_4 = m4 - 4 * m3 * m1 + 6 * m2 * m1^2 - 3 * m1^4,
    skewness = central_moment_3 / sd^3,
    kurtosis = central_moment_4 / sd^4
  )
```

```{r}
response_names <- c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "kurtosis")
response_summary <- analysis |>
  summarise(across(all_of(response_names),
                   list(min = min, q1 = ~ quantile(.x, .25), median = median,
                        mean = mean, q3 = ~ quantile(.x, .75), max = max,
                        sd = sd))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("response", ".value"), names_pattern = "(.*)_(min|q1|median|mean|q3|max|sd)")
response_summary |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
predictor_dist <- analysis |>
  mutate(Fr_condition = if_else(is.infinite(Fr), "Inf", as.character(Fr))) |>
  group_by(Re, Fr_condition) |>
  summarise(n = n(), 
            St_min = min(St), 
            St_max = max(St), 
            St_levels = n_distinct(St), .groups = "drop")
predictor_dist |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
response_long <- analysis |>
  select(Re, Fr, St, all_of(response_names)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(response_names), names_to = "response", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(Fr_condition = if_else(is.infinite(Fr), "Inf", as.character(Fr)),
         log_value = log(value), 
         log_St = log(St),
         response = fct_relevel(response, "mean", "sd", "skewness", "kurtosis"))

ggplot(response_long, aes(log_value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 18, color = "white", fill = "darkblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ response, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Log scale summary statistics", 
       y = "Count", 
       title = "Distribution of summary statistics on log scale") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 8
ggplot(response_long, aes(log_St, log_value, color = factor(Re))) +
  geom_point(alpha = .8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = .6) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(response), cols = vars(Fr_condition), scales = "free_y",
             switch = "y") +
  labs(x = "log(St)", 
       y = "Log scale summary statistics", 
       color = "Re level",
       title = "Relation between log-St and responses, with different levels of Fr and Re",
       subtitle = "Columns represent Fr value") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "grey65", fill = NA, linewidth = .45),
    panel.spacing.y = grid::unit(1.1, "lines"),
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey88", color = "grey55"),
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(face = "bold", angle = 0),
    strip.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

## Response transformations

```{r}
#| label: fig-skew
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of each response on the raw scale (top) and log scale (bottom), with the sample skewness of each."
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8
skew_long <- data |>
  select(all_of(unname(responses))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "response", values_to = "Raw") |>
  mutate(Log = log(Raw)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Raw, Log), names_to = "scale") |>
  mutate(skew = if_else(scale == "Raw", skew_raw[response], skew_log[response]),
         panel = sprintf("%s (%s)\nskew = %.2f", response_labels[response], scale, skew))
panel_levels <- c(sprintf("%s (Raw)\nskew = %.2f", response_labels, skew_raw),
                  sprintf("%s (Log)\nskew = %.2f", response_labels, skew_log))

ggplot(skew_long, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 18, color = "white", fill = "darkblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(panel, levels = panel_levels), nrow = 2, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-boxcox
#| tbl-cap: 'Estimated Box-Cox $\lambda$ for each response, with 95% profile-likelihood intervals. $\lambda = 0$ is the log transform.'
bc |>
  transmute(Response = unname(response_labels[response]),
            Estimate = sprintf("%.2f", lambda),
            `95% interval` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", lower, upper)) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxcox
#| fig-cap: 'Box-Cox profile log-likelihood for each response under the cubic comparison model, relative to its maximum. Values of $\lambda$ above the dotted line form the 95% interval; the dashed line marks $\lambda = 0$ (the log).'
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| fig-width: 8
bind_rows(bc_profiles, .id = "response") |>
  filter(loglik > -8) |>
  mutate(response = factor(response_labels[response], levels = response_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(lambda, loglik)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(color = "darkblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ response, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Log-likelihood\n(relative to max)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = grid::unit(1.5, "lines"))
```
